pageData.title: The Viceroyalty of New Spain
pageData.para1: The Viceroyalty of New Spain. The Viceroyalty of New Spain was the first of the four viceroyalties that Spain created to govern its conquered lands in the New World. Established in 1535, fourteen years after the fall of Tenochtitlan, it initially embraced all Spanish-controlled land north of the Isthmus of Panama, and later grew to take in upper and lower California, the future southwestern United States, the Gulf coast eastward to Florida, Spain's Caribbean possessions, and from 1565 even the newly conquered Philippines. Administered from Mexico City for three centuries, this administration matters deeply because it was the first great template of Spanish rule in the Americas, integrating the hemisphere into global commerce through an economy based almost entirely on mining and ranching, while its viceroys sponsored the conversion of the Native population to Christianity and built an array of educational institutions.
pageData.para2: The viceroy, appointed by the Spanish Crown, was technically the supreme authority, yet in practice the considerable independence of governors and royal audiencias in the subordinate regions confined his real power largely to central and southern Mexico. The first viceroy, Antonio de Mendoza, who ruled from 1535 to 1549, dispatched Francisco Coronado on his expedition northward while ameliorating some of the worst abuses of the conquistadores and supporting the church's work with the Native population. That mission came at a terrible cost: during the first hundred years of Spanish rule, the Indigenous population of New Spain collapsed from an estimated 25 million to 1 million through maltreatment, disease, and the disruption of their cultures, while a casta hierarchy - famously catalogued in the viceroyalty's paintings - stratified society by ancestry. After a period of decline in the late seventeenth century, distinguished viceroys such as Bucareli and Revillagigedo revived the administration and pushed settlement overland into California to counter Russian and British interest; the viceroyalty weathered the early independence risings of Hidalgo and Morelos, only to succumb to Agustin de Iturbide's coalition in 1821.

pageData.title: The Haitian Revolution
pageData.para1: The Haitian Revolution. The Haitian Revolution was the only successful slave revolt in history: an anti-slavery and anti-colonial insurrection that convulsed the French colony of Saint-Domingue from 1791 to 1804 and led directly to the founding of an independent state. On the eve of the uprising the colony held some 556,000 people - roughly half a million enslaved Africans alongside 32,000 European colonists and 24,000 affranchis, free people of color - and the enslaved majority endured backbreaking workdays on the sugar plantations, often dying from injuries and exhaustion. When revolution broke out in France, the colonists' rival factions fought over the Declaration of the Rights of Man, and in October 1790 the affranchi Vincent Oge led an unsuccessful revolt; the following year the enslaved themselves rose, and the former slave Toussaint Louverture became their great leader. This revolution matters because it shattered the foundations of Atlantic slavery and terrified slaveholding regimes across the Western Hemisphere.
pageData.para2: Toussaint proved a master strategist: first fighting alongside Spain, he abandoned his Spanish allies when the French Republic abolished slavery in 1794, rose to commander-in-chief of the island by 1797, defeated Spanish and British forces, conquered Santo Domingo in 1801, and had himself named governor-general for life. Napoleon answered by sending his brother-in-law, General Charles Leclerc, with an experienced army to restore French rule; Toussaint struggled for months, agreed to an armistice in May 1802, and was then seized and exiled to France. The fighting continued under Jean-Jacques Dessalines and Henry Christophe, whose forces prevailed over the French, and in 1804 Dessalines declared Haiti independent, giving the territory its new name. The price of survival was steep: France withheld recognition until 1825, and then only in exchange for an indemnity of 100 million francs that - together with diplomatic isolation - burdened the young republic's development for generations.

pageData.title: The Mexican War of Independence
pageData.para1: The Mexican War of Independence. The Mexican War of Independence was an armed conflict that lasted from 1810 to 1821, ending three centuries of Spanish rule. It began with the Grito de Dolores - the 'Cry of Dolores' - uttered on September 16, 1810 by Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla, the parish priest of Dolores, a highly educated creole who had read the Enlightenment writers. Calling upon peasants and unemployed miners to rise against the viceroyalty's government, Hidalgo demanded not only liberation from Spain but the abolition of slavery and tribute, the redistribution of wealth, and the return of land to the Indigenous people, and he marched under a banner of the Virgin of Guadalupe, proclaimed the rebellion's guardian and protector. His movement gathered a huge popular mob-army, but after much reckless pillage and bloodshed it was checked; Hidalgo was captured and executed on July 30, 1811. His 'cry' became the cry of independence, commemorated each year on the night of September 16.
pageData.para2: Jose Maria Morelos, another revolutionary priest and an organizer of artisans and peasants, took up the campaign with clear sociopolitical objectives: an end to slavery and the casta system, the abolition of Indigenous tribute, and independence from Spain. In his Sentiments of the Nation, composed to guide the congress he had charged with producing a constitution, Morelos listed twenty-three points he believed would create a strong nation capable of protecting all its people; but after Morelos's death his follower, the casta Vicente Guerrero, continued guerrilla operations against Spanish authorities for several more years, until Agustin de Iturbide - a royalist creole officer who had distinguished himself in the campaigns against Hidalgo and Morelos - changed sides. In 1821 Iturbide formed an agreement with the rebel leader Vicente Guerrero and issued the Plan of Iguala, built on the Three Guarantees of independence, religion, and equality: Mexico would be independent of Spain, Roman Catholicism the official religion, and criollos and peninsulares equal in rights. Their Army of the Three Guarantees entered Mexico City in triumph, and on August 24, 1821, with the signing of the Treaty of Cordoba, Spain finally recognized the independence of Mexico.

pageData.title: New France
pageData.para1: New France. New France was the French colonial empire in North America, claimed for King Francis I when Jacques Cartier entered the Gulf of St. Lawrence in 1534. After an early colony near Quebec failed, the French fur trade with the First Nations took root, and Samuel de Champlain founded Port-Royal, the first French colony in North America, then in 1608 began the settlement of Quebec on a commanding site controlling the narrowing of the St. Lawrence. New France matters because its economy rested on the fur trade and on alliance with Indigenous nations rather than on mass settlement: the Company of New France held a monopoly of the trade in return for bringing settlers, missionaries aimed to convert the First Nations and excluded Huguenots, and vigorous young men slipped away from the seigneurial estates - where habitants farmed land granted by seigneurs in return for dues - to become coureurs de bois in the forests.
pageData.para2: Under royal rule the colony pushed far beyond the St. Lawrence: Louis Jolliet explored the Mississippi until he was sure it flowed into the Gulf of Mexico, and in 1699 Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville founded Louisiana, another part of New France. War with England shadowed the colony from the start - during King William's War a New England fleet under Sir William Phips seized Acadia, though Quebec defied his attack - and in 1700 and 1701 peace was made between the Iroquois and New France. The end came in the Seven Years' War: when peace was made by the Treaty of Paris in 1763, all New France east of the Mississippi, outside the environs of New Orleans, was ceded to Great Britain, and France kept only the two little islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon. French culture, however, survived the conquest - above all in Quebec, and in the Louisiana that passed through Spanish and French hands before ending up with the United States in 1804.

pageData.title: The Mexican Empire & First Republic
pageData.para1: The Mexican Empire and First Republic. The Mexican Empire was the brief monarchy that spanned the transition from colony to independent republic. When Agustin de Iturbide's Army of the Three Guarantees secured independence in 1821, independence from the former mother country had been the only glue binding republicans and monarchists together; in 1822 Iturbide crowned himself Emperor Agustin I, and towns across Mexico swore recognition and obedience to 'Agustin Primero' on December 8, 1822 - the celebrated Poblano prints record those oaths, printed on sheets of gold, silver, and bronze alloy. The experiment collapsed within months: revolts found their pretext, General Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna among the rebel leaders, and Agustin was forced to reconvene congress and abdicate; in 1824 he returned from European exile, but was arrested and shot.
pageData.para2: The constitution of 1824 made Mexico a federal republic of nineteen states, four territories, and the Mexico City federal district, and Guadalupe Victoria, a leader of the independence movement, was elected its first president. But the pendulum of power swung between Centralists, who favored a strong national army and Roman Catholicism as the exclusive religion, and Federalists, who favored limited central government and nearly autonomous states - a struggle dominated for a third of a century by the charismatic Santa Anna. When Santa Anna's new constitution of 1836 eliminated all vestiges of states' rights, Texas revolted; Santa Anna trapped and eliminated the Alamo garrison, but was defeated and captured by Texas forces in April 1836. The United States annexed the Republic of Texas in 1845, Mexican and U.S. patrols clashed in April 1846, and the Mexican-American War that followed ended in 1848 with Mexico giving up its claims to Texas and ceding the territories of today's California, Utah, Nevada, New Mexico, Arizona, and beyond - the humiliating dismemberment of almost half the national territory.

pageData.title: The Colonial Caribbean (Spanish, French, British, Dutch)
pageData.para1: The Colonial Caribbean. The colonial Caribbean - the Spanish Main and the West Indian islands - was the first American world conquered by Europe. Spain settled Puerto Rico and then Cuba in 1511, introduced cattle, horses, and mules, and created plantations growing sugar cane, just as the Portuguese had done on Atlantic islands like Madeira; native peoples were ruthlessly robbed, butchered, or enslaved, and perhaps two million African slaves were shipped to the Spanish Main in the 16th and 17th centuries. The riches were guarded jealously - Havana, from 1610, boasted the largest shipyard in the Americas - but the other empires muscled in: the English planted St. Kitts in 1623, Barbados in 1624, and Nevis, Antigua, and Montserrat by 1632, the French took Martinique and Guadeloupe in 1635, and from 1599 Dutch ships loaded salt at Araya.
pageData.para2: The seventeenth century became the great age of the buccaneers: when the English seized Jamaica with its wonderful natural harbours in 1655, the entire Spanish Main lay open to attack, and privateers sponsored by the colonial authorities struck its ports - Henry Morgan sacked Panama in 1671 and ransomed Portobelo in 1680, pirates raided Veracruz in 1683 and made off with the loot meant for a treasure fleet, and a French naval and pirate force captured Cartagena in 1697, the last major buccaneer raid. The islands produced sugar, tobacco, coffee, and cotton through the horrific business of slavery, and they matter because their plantations bound Europe, Africa, and the Americas into a single Atlantic economy. French rule in Saint-Domingue ended in 1804 with the only successful slave revolt in history, and through the 1820s the Latin American nations declared independence from Spain, with rebel forces besieging and taking even Cartagena in 1815 and 1821.

pageData.title: The Thirteen Colonies & British America
pageData.para1: The Thirteen Colonies & British America. The Thirteen Colonies were the British settlements planted along the Atlantic coast of North America between 1607 and 1732. It began when the Virginia Company established Jamestown in 1607 - a colony that nearly perished in the 'Starving Time' of 1609-10, when as many as 350 of the estimated 500 colonists died - and was saved when John Rolfe's tobacco seed from Bermuda took to the fertile Chesapeake soil, Virginia soon outstripping the West Indies as the main exporter of tobacco to Europe. In 1620 the Mayflower brought 102 Puritan separatists, the 'Pilgrims', to Massachusetts, and in 1630 John Winthrop led the Puritan 'Great Migration' to New England; the chain of colonies was completed in 1732, when Georgia was established as a buffer zone between the Carolinas and the hostile Spanish. These colonies matter because they developed robust traditions of local self-governance and representative assemblies, elected by propertied citizens, which the colonists prized as the shield of their rights.
pageData.para2: The colonies fell into three administrative categories - charter, royal, and proprietary - Virginia becoming the first royal colony when its company went bankrupt in 1624; New England was founded primarily by Puritans seeking religious freedom, while the Chesapeake drew poor young fortune-seekers seduced by the promise of the lucrative tobacco trade. From the earliest days of Jamestown the English also waged war with the Native Americans upon whose lands they were encroaching. Operating under British imperial mercantilism, the colonies long enjoyed considerable freedom from London, but the expensive French and Indian War changed the imperial mood: taxes such as the Sugar Act (1764) and the Stamp Act (1765), aimed at raising revenue from the colonies, outraged the colonists and catalyzed a resistance that forged a shared political identity among the thirteen colonies - and led directly to the American Revolutionary War.

pageData.title: The American Revolution & Early Republic
pageData.para1: The American Revolution & Early Republic. The American Revolution was the insurrection fought between 1775 and 1783 through which thirteen of Great Britain's North American colonies threw off British rule and established the sovereign United States of America. It began on April 19, 1775, when British regulars skirmished with American provincials first at Lexington - where a British force of 700 faced 77 local minutemen - and then at Concord, after Britain's attempts to assert greater control over colonial affairs ended a long period of salutary neglect. On July 4, 1776, the Continental Congress approved the Declaration of Independence, written chiefly by Thomas Jefferson, announcing the separation of the thirteen colonies; the final vote for separation had actually come two days earlier, on July 2. This revolution matters because what began as a civil war within the British Empire became an international war - France joining the colonies in 1778 and Spain in 1779 - and turned colonial resistance into a new nation founded on an articulated ideal of self-government.
pageData.para2: The Continental Army commanded by George Washington, assisted by those crucial French and Spanish alliances, fought until the major fighting ended in 1781 and the peace treaty of 1783 recognized independence. The young republic first governed itself under the Articles of Confederation, but the Articles proved unworkable - the central government lacked essential powers - so delegates to the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia wrote the U.S. Constitution in 1787, the oldest written national constitution still in use. It created a federal system of balanced branches with checks and balances, and its first ten amendments, the Bill of Rights, guaranteed fundamental rights and liberties to individuals. Yet the early republic also faced severe challenges - national debt, partisan polarization, and the unresolved moral contradiction of chattel slavery and indigenous displacement in a nation dedicated to liberty.

pageData.title: The Confederation of Canada
pageData.para1: The Confederation of Canada. The Confederation of Canada was the process by which the three British North American colonies of the mid-19th century - the Province of Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick - united to form the Dominion of Canada. Fueled by the fear of possible American aggression and by economic ambition, politicians and the public debated merging the colonies into one self-governing confederation; with British support, representatives negotiated the terms of their union at conferences in Charlottetown and Quebec, where Sir John A. Macdonald and Cartier joined with their chief opponent George Brown to further the scheme. The result was the British North America Act, passed in 1867 and put into effect on July 1 - now celebrated as Canada Day - creating a new country of four provinces: Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, with the former Province of Canada split into Ontario and Quebec. This union matters because it created the stable federal framework from which a transcontinental nation would grow.
pageData.para2: Confederation did not yet mean independence: the new law established Canada as a semi-independent 'Dominion' of the British Empire, without full autonomy, and the journey toward full independence continued for decades - after the First World War, Canada joined the other dominions in seeking formal recognition of its independence, reaching a milestone in 1931. Macdonald, the Dominion's first prime minister (1867-73, 1878-91), dominated the early decades: forced to resign in 1873 by the Pacific Scandal - in which his government was accused of taking bribes over the Pacific railway contract - he returned five years later and applied his policy of trade protectionism swiftly and thoroughly. Over the decades that followed, Canada expanded across the continent, absorbing vast northern and western territories and additional provinces, and transformed itself from a cluster of colonies into a modern transcontinental nation.
